top_choice_rationale: Adonis (P001) is my first choice on the common criteria. A poetry that remakes the idiom of Arabic verse through myth, fragmentation and a sustained argument with inherited forms is a language-level renewal, which I judge the more durable kind of distinctiveness. The oeuvre is long and fully formed and can be judged as a whole now. The citation is anchored in the poetry, with the poetics named only as the project that informs it, so critical influence does not become a second ground for the prize. The main limits are stated openly. The prosodic, diction-level and allusive core is not directly testable by me and rests on translations and secondary accounts. Whether the later decades deepen the project or repeat it is not settled by the supplied record. The three-member overlap on this proposal is not merit and I do not count it. Cărtărescu (P002) is a close second. The assessability argument and the late-volume test apply to both candidates, and I could support him if confidence in the Arabic poems cannot be reached. Carson (P003) is a serious candidate, but her whole-oeuvre case is not yet established beyond the named works and her object-dependent forms. I rank her above no award because the translation limits apply to every candidate and do not by themselves justify P000.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. No documented personal, institutional or translation connection to Adonis, Cărtărescu, Carson or any other shortlisted writer. For transparency, my scholarly work on modern poetry, the literary fragment and exile literature is thematically close to the fragmentation and tradition-argument in the Adonis entry. That is context, not evidence of preference, and it is disclosed here without adjudication.
